checked_and_found_correct: Every console transcript was re-run byte-for-byte by three reviewers on Node 24.18.0, commander@15.0.0 and burgee@0.9.2. The program block is byte-identical to the file the repro writes.

The causal chain behind `"data":null` was checked against the façade source. `_emitResult` writes `data: value ?? null`, and commander actions return nothing. Under `--mcp`, the tool-call invoke captures `writeOut` but not `console.log`, so the prose line reaches the JSON-RPC stream (1 non-JSON line before the second edit, 0 after).

The MCP defect has its root cause read, not inferred. `optionArgs` in `packages/burgee/src/mcp.ts` pushes `--${name}` (the camelCased key) and ignores the advertised `flag`. The file is unchanged between tag `burgee@0.9.2` and origin/main.

Compat oracle re-run twice, independently, at burgee `6377897aaf`: `burgee/commander` 1360 / 1360 against a control of 1360 / 1360 (1 skipped on this OS). The vendored suite is commander v15.0.0, 110 files.

Exit codes: the façade keeps commander's `1` for usage errors because burgee's E1 mapping applies only when `exit` is injected. The native syntax exits `2`, verified with a `defineCommand` that declares `effects`.

The second-edit recipe works for MCP. Tool calls re-enter through `root.parseAsync(argvOf(...))`, but the server process's own argv carries `--mcp`, so `machine` is true for every call. The only misfire anyone could construct is a contrived `count -- --json`, and the article already calls the check crude.
Install matrix: npm, yarn 1, yarn 4 (PnP), pnpm 10 and 12, bun, `require()` on Node 24, `import { program }`, and a `bin` install with a shebang. All of them run the swapped program.

All 43 spec rows pass the stage-6 detector's own parser, digit comparison and 60s timeout. `yarn1-node22-exit` throws when no Node 22 binary exists, so on a bare runner it reports as a failed command rather than passing vacuously.

Framing: no banned vocabulary. The article quotes burgee's own unmet `lighter-than-commander` gate, discloses that `.effects()` is a one-way door, and names the case where commander alone is the smaller choice.
The 9-reviewer devto-review gate passed in both rounds with zero blockers (gate score 8.9, then 9.0; Technical 9.5, Checklist 10.0 both rounds).

Cover: `validate-hooks` has 0 errors, `verify-hook-facts` has 0 numbers missing from the body (1360 found), and `cover-check` passes mechanically (1 mark rendering, 0 glyphs clipped by the 1200×630 crop). Both crops were inspected.

growth_hook.why: The title fits the formula at 67 characters: named target, concrete count, and a true claim against the author's own tool. The body delivers exactly that. Paragraph 2 now carries the thesis on its own ('One import describes the CLI to an agent; answering takes a `return`'), so a reader who stops after the diff still leaves with the idea. The cover's `data: null` over '1360 of 1360 tests green' states the paradox that the grade section resolves. The closing question about regex-scraped output is specific enough to draw war stories. Held below 10 by the chassis' fixed `getting-started` label, which undersells a piece written for maintainers.

security_correctness.why: Read as technical correctness, since there is no security claim. Every transcript was re-derived, and every causal explanation matches the façade source: the null envelope, the leaked prose line, the camelCased MCP argument, and the exit-code split. The TypeScript and Node-22 additions were probed and hold. The remaining notes are wording, not substance: the TS sentence leaves out that `node16` works in an ESM package, and the article says 'cannot see the subpath' rather than enumerating every resolver that can.

structure_framing_voice.why: All seven H2s serve one argument. The null opens the piece, 'Where one import stops' pays it off, and 'What the grade covers' names the line it turns on: the grade measures what you keep, and both defects sit in what you gain. The framing toward commander would survive its maintainers reading it: the unmet gate is quoted against ourselves, the lock-in is disclosed, and there is a closing case for commander alone. After round 1 the tutorial can be followed end to end. A semicolon-splice rhythm was flagged and thinned.

compatibility.why: The matrix a commander maintainer would hit is now covered, and each part was verified independently: four package managers (plus yarn 4 PnP and pnpm 12), `require()`, TypeScript resolution, and the Node floor with its real consequence (yarn 1 refuses on Node 22, npm only warns). The install is pinned to the version measured, and the 0.10.0 re-pin is recorded. All ten frontmatter keys are present, `reading_time_minutes` matches the repo's own computation, cover stems derive from the slug, and every outbound link returns 2xx. The ESLint and Oxlint rows of pass 3 do not apply to a CLI library.

reproducibility.why: All 43 spec rows re-ran green under the detector's parser and timeout. Each behavioural row is a single probe of a committed script that builds the article's exact program. A stranger starting from an empty directory can now reproduce every transcript from the article alone: the install block creates package.json, both dependencies, the ESM flag and the fixture. The compat oracle was re-run, not quoted. The remaining gaps are environmental and house-wide: the `../burgee` rows and the Node-22 row need a sibling checkout and a Node 22 binary on the weekly runner.

Defects found in burgee 0.9.2 while writing, for the owner. Disclosed in the article: MCP tool calls pass multi-word options camelCased (`mcp.ts` `optionArgs`); completions offer `--no-<flag>` spellings the program refuses. Found but not in the article: the `burgee` bin (`dist/cli.js`) ships without a shebang, so `npx burgee migrate` fails in the shell; the README 'Start here' example omits `effects`, and `defineCommand` throws on it in 0.9.2; `agent-surfaces.mdx`, `vs/commander.mdx` and the package README FAQ still say undeclared commands are not served over MCP.
